food.text: Chinese immigrants arriving in Peru at the end of the 19th century gave the country arroz chaufa, a fried rice dish with vegetables, usually including scallions, eggs, and chicken. It is cooked quickly at high heat, often in a wok with soy sauce and oil. It belongs to the Chinese Peruvian cuisine called chifa.

The first group of Asians came to Peru in 1849 on the Danish ship Federico Guillermo, brought to replace slavery as part of the plan to abolish it in 1854. During the next 25 years, 100,000 Chinese arrived on eight-year contracts from Macao, Hong Kong, Canton and Fujian. They were hired for sugar cane fields, rice fields, extracting guano and constructing the railroads in the Andes, in semi-slavery working conditions.

Italians in Peru later took up the cultivation of grapes for wine. In 1905, 83% of wine production came from wineries founded and managed by Italians. Some grape varieties imported from Italy were introduced in Peru in this context.

In the late 19th century Peru experienced an influx of African and Asian immigrants. Chinese immigrants created lomo saltado, a stir-fry of beef, onions, tomatoes, and French fries. It has become a popular dish in Peru and globally.

The Puelches raised horses on the eastern slopes of the Andes and traded them for weapons and alcoholic beverages. Through this trade they became one of the main food providers of the isolated exclave of Valdivia. The Argentine and Chilean military campaigns of the second half of the 19th century, the conquest of the Desert and the occupation of Araucanía, brought a definitive end to it. In the 1880s the Argentine Army displaced indigenous communities from the area.

The butifarra, a pork sandwich typical of Lima, is mentioned by Pedro Paz Soldán y Unanue in his Dictionary of Peruanisms from 1884. He indicated that it was sold in chinganas, bullfights, and occasionally on the street.

During the same late 19th-century influx of African and Asian immigrants, African slaves introduced dishes such as tacu-tacu. It is a mix of rice and beans that was fried and served with steak or eggs.
The butifarrero was the vendor who hawked butifarras. By the late 19th century, butifarreros moved to the exit of the Plaza de toros de Acho to offer chicken butifarras.

art.text: Frederic Edwin Church's The Heart of the Andes is an oil painting of an idealized Andes landscape, more than five feet high and almost ten feet wide. When it was exhibited in New York City in 1859 it was a sensation. It established Church as the foremost landscape painter in the United States.

The Andes of Ecuador, painted in 1855, was Frederic Edwin Church's first major painting and his largest work at the time. It combined different climate zones into one image, from snowy mountains in the distance to grasslands in the mid-ground and tropical flora in the foreground.

In the late 18th and early 19th century, Peruvian architecture took a neoclassical turn. Builders returned to Greco-Roman styles, using straight lines, simplicity, columns with Corinthian capitals and a triangular frontispiece. Examples include the altar and towers of the Cathedral of Lima and the Presbyter Matías Maestro Cemetery.

The Heart of the Andes was shown by itself in eastern U.S. cities, in rooms with special lighting and decorative elements reminiscent of the depicted landscape. The painting stood in a floor-standing frame. The public, enchanted by its detail, was willing to wait in line and pay a 25-cent entrance fee.

Church did not paint one real view in The Heart of the Andes. He synthesized many Andes topographies, from Mount Chimborazo to a plain and a jungle. The details include numerous animals and signs of human settlement, such as people visiting a cross in the left foreground.

Church traveled in Ecuador and Colombia in 1853 and 1857, financed by businessman Cyrus West Field, who wanted the paintings to lure investors to his South American ventures. Church was inspired by Alexander von Humboldt and his 1845 treatise Kosmos, and he retraced Humboldt's travels in South America.

Frederic Edwin Church, inspired by Humboldt and his 1845 Kosmos, traveled in Ecuador and Colombia in 1853 and 1857. He retraced Humboldt's travels in South America. His painting The Heart of the Andes, shown in New York in 1859, was a sensation.

In the second volume of Kosmos, Alexander von Humboldt held that art is among the highest expressions of the love of nature. He challenged artists to portray the "physiognomy" of the landscape. Church answered that challenge with his Andes paintings.

The mountains in The Andes of Ecuador, probably Tungurahua at left and Cotopaxi at right, run along two lines that converge near the painting's center. This follows Humboldt's observation that the Andes stand in two lines from north to south around the Chota Valley, separated by a plateau.

Humboldt encouraged painters to make sketches in the field, a practice not common at the time. The Andes of Ecuador shows the influence of Church's own sketches made in northern Ecuador and southern Colombia.

Church's 1855 painting subdued its details with strong light and left out Chimborazo, then thought to be the world's highest mountain. A critic in Harper's Weekly said all detail and shape were lost in the vastness of the gorges. In 1859 Church cataloged plants and topography more clearly, ending with Chimborazo, under more naturalistic lighting.

Alexander von Humboldt's 1845 treatise Kosmos described in its second volume how landscape painting influences the study of nature. It challenged artists to portray the "physiognomy" of the landscape. Frederic Edwin Church traveled in Ecuador and Colombia in 1853 and 1857, retracing Humboldt's South American journeys.

Church sold The Heart of the Andes to William Tilden Blodgett for $10,000, then the highest price paid for a work by a living American artist. Church reserved the right to resell it if offered at least $20,000. Albert Bierstadt later passed both prices, selling The Rocky Mountains, Lander's Peak for $25,000 in 1865.

The Andes of Ecuador was shown at the Boston Athenæum in early 1855, where Henry Thoreau saw it. Railway tycoon William H. Osborn bought it, and it stayed in his family until 1965. The Reynolda House Museum of American Art acquired it in 1966.

war.text: In January 1817, General José de San Martín led an army out of Mendoza to cross the Andes and invade Chile. The successful crossing took 21 days through heights averaging 3,000 meters. It has been compared to Hannibal's and Napoleon's crossings of the Alps.

The War of the Pacific ran from 1879 to 1884, pitting Chile against a Bolivian–Peruvian alliance. It ended in a Chilean victory, and Chile gained a large amount of resource-rich territory from Peru and Bolivia. The war demonstrated Chile's military-technological superiority over its opponents.

The Chiriguanos kept their lands in the Andes foothills of southeastern Bolivia from the 16th to the 19th centuries. They fended off first the Inca Empire, then the Spanish Empire, and later independent Bolivia. They were finally subjugated in 1892.

The Battle of Ayacucho in 1824 secured the independence of Peru and definitively ended Spanish rule in South America. The Peruvian War of Independence itself was a series of military conflicts lasting from 1809 to 1826.

San Martín crossed the Andes in 1817 with 4,000 men, but he ultimately lost one-third of them during the trek. The army was split in two: the main division used the Pass of Los Patos, while a secondary division took the more southerly Uspallata Pass under Juan Gregorio de Las Heras.

In January 1892 a 28-year-old named Chapiaguasu, who styled himself Apiaguaiki Tumpa (Eunuch of God), led a Chiriguano rebellion at the mission of Santa Rosa de Cuevo. He said he had been sent to save the Chiriguanos from Christianity and the Franciscan missionaries. His army of 1,300 failed in its attack on the mission on January 21.

After the Chilean military defeated the Mapuche in 1883, it began to restrict them to reservations. Chilean efforts were then made to convert the Mapuche to Catholicism. Before that, the Mapuche had prevented conquest by the Incan and Spanish Empires.

On February 13, 1817, San Martín and Bernardo O'Higgins entered Santiago after crossing 500 kilometers of mountain range. Royalist forces had moved north to avoid them, but one royalist leader stayed behind with 1,500 men at a valley called Chacabuco. This led to the Battle of Chacabuco.

At the Battle of Kuruyuki, a Creole force of 50 soldiers, 140 militia and 1,500 friendly Indians with bows and arrows killed more than 600 Chiriguanos. Their own losses were only four killed. Afterward the army massacred Chiriguanos who surrendered and sold women and children into slavery.

After Bolívar's project failed, Peruvian pressure led to talks on withdrawing the Gran Colombian troops occupying Callao. The division mutinied, and on February 16, 1827, command of the Real Felipe Fortress passed to Peruvian authorities. Peru then regained full sovereignty.

The army's main food was valdiviano, a dish of dried meat or charqui, sliced raw onion, potatoes, and boiling water. Designated soldiers carried forty tons of charqui, maize cakes, meat, brandy against the nighttime cold, and garlic and onion to stimulate appetite. They also drove over 4,000 cattle for the rest of the campaign.

Apiaguaiki was captured and, on March 29, 1892, tortured and executed by Bolivian authorities. His movement resembled other Millenarian movements of the time, such as the Ghost Dance in the United States and the Boxer Rebellion in China.

literature.text: In the 19th century a shift allowed more women to become authors in Latin America. Peruvian writers such as Clorinda Matto de Turner and Mercedes Cabello de Carbonera became prominent. Women writers often wrote about inequalities left over from colonialism, including the marginalization and oppression of Indigenous peoples, slaves, and women.
The Peruvian Naturalist author Clorinda Matto de Turner wrote Aves sin nido, published in 1889. It is considered one of the most important novels of "indigenismo" in the 19th century.
The general crisis that followed the War of the Pacific gave rise to Modernism in Peru. Its best-known exponents were José Santos Chocano and José María Eguren.

Peruvian Naturalist Mercedes Cabello de Carbonera wrote Blanca Sol in 1888. The novel criticized the lack of practical work options that women faced in her society. She is described as a Naturalist trail-blazer.

In his 1905 thesis Character of the Literature of Independent Peru, Jose de la Riva Agüero called the Pre-Hispanic literary tradition "insufficient". He saw it as unimportant in forming any new literary tradition. Scholars only rescued it from obscurity in the 20th century.
Juana Manuela Gorriti (1818–1892) was an Argentinian Romantic writer who penned novels and short stories, including La hija del mashorquero in 1860. She also directed a literary circle in Peru.

Adolfo Vienrich compiled Quechua tales in the early 1900s. Tarmap Pacha Huaray, translated as Azucenas quechuas or Quechuan lilies, appeared in 1905. Tarmapap Pachahuarainin, or Quechuan fables, followed in 1906.

Pedro Cieza de León composed El señorío de los Incas between 1548 and 1550, but it was first published only in 1873. Its fourth volume, a series of books on the wars among the Spanish, was published in 1877 and 1881.

Aurora Cáceres is a Peruvian author who, according to the source, has not received the critical attention she deserves. She wrote two novels and a dozen works of non-fiction prose. She is named among the notable writers of Peru's Modernism.

Clorinda Matto de Turner also wrote Indole, Herencia, and El Conspirador: autobiografia de un hombre publico. These works are cited as examples of writing that discussed the hypocrisy of the dominant class and institutions in the new nations. They also criticized government corruption.

science.text: In 1853 and 1857, the American painter Frederic Edwin Church traveled in Ecuador and Colombia, retracing the South American journeys of the Prussian naturalist Alexander von Humboldt. Humboldt was among the last of the great scientific generalists, and his fame became similar to that of Albert Einstein a century later.

The explorer Francisco Moreno was a pioneer who studied the Patagonian Andes in the 19th century, and the Perito Moreno Glacier is named after him. The glacier is 30 km long and is one of 48 glaciers fed by the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, the world's third largest reserve of fresh water.

Physalis peruviana, a nightshade plant reportedly native to Chile and Peru, was cultivated in South Africa since at least the start of the 19th century. Early settlers of the Cape of Good Hope grew it before 1807, and not long after it was introduced to Australia, New Zealand and various Pacific islands.

In the second volume of his 1845 treatise Kosmos, Humboldt described the influence of landscape painting on the study of the natural world. He held that art is among the highest expressions of the love of nature, and challenged artists to portray the 'physiognomy' of the landscape.

In 1879, the British Chilean Navy captain Juan Tomás Rogers was the first non-indigenous person to sight the glacier. He named it Francisco Gormaz, after the Director of the Hydrographic Office of the Chilean Navy, which sponsored the expedition.

In 1899, after long years of research, compilation of archaeological material and surveys of the area, Lieutenant Iglesias of the Argentine Hydrographic Institute named the glacier Perito Moreno. He did so in homage to Francisco Moreno.

Despite its English name Cape gooseberry, Physalis peruviana is not botanically related to the true gooseberries of the genus Ribes. Sources since the mid-19th century attribute the name to its early growth at the Cape, while the idea that it refers to the calyx being like a cape does not appear before the mid-20th century.

When European explorers rediscovered the Gate of the Sun at Tiwanaku in the mid-19th century, it lay horizontally with a large crack through it. The 1851 folio Antigüedades peruanas used an engraving of the gateway as its frontispiece.

Tree rings on the shorelines show no major damming and rupture events of the Brazo Rico from about 1635 until the 20th century. At the end of the 19th century the glacier's front began moving toward the opposite bank, and in 1899 it was 750 meters from the Magallanes peninsula.

politics.text: After independence, all of Spain's former territories agreed to set their limits by the principle of uti possidetis juris, which treated the Spanish borders of 1810 as the borders of the new republics. Conflicting claims between the new countries nonetheless escalated to armed conflicts on several occasions.

Following the Spanish American wars of independence (1810–1825), the Aymara became subjects to the new nations of Bolivia and Peru. After the War of the Pacific (1879–1883), Chile annexed territory inhabited by the Aymara population.

On October 26, 1858, war began between Peru and Ecuador. According to the Peruvian plenipotentiary Juan Celestino Cavero, the Ecuadorian government had decided to settle its foreign debt with England by ceding Peruvian Amazonian territories.

The War of the Pacific, also called the nitrate war, pitted Chile against an alliance of Bolivia and Peru. It was precipitated by a northward incursion by Chile to control sources of guano in Bolivia's Litoral province and Peru's Tarapacá province, and it left the Aymara politically separated between three nations.

After Bolívar withdrew in 1826, liberal and nationalist elements in Peru put an end to the Bolivarian regime in January 1827. The new government dismissed the Colombian troops and expelled the Colombian diplomatic agent, Cristóbal Armero.

After a successful blockade of the Ecuadorian coast and the occupation of Guayaquil, the Treaty of Mapasingue was signed, also called the Franco-Castile Treaty. It recognized the validity of the Royal Decree of 1802 and the uti possidetis of 1810.

On October 22, 1907, Colombia unilaterally declared the modus vivendi of 1906 ended and appointed authorities in Putumayo. In response, the Peruvian Foreign Ministry asked Julio C. Arana to help with his employees to repel a possible Colombian invasion.

On September 21, 1810, the seminary founded in Mérida in 1785 was elevated to the Royal University of San Buenaventura of Mérida de los Caballeros. This entitled it to confer junior and senior degrees in Philosophy, Medicine, Civil and Canonical Law, and Theology.

In 1826 Simón Bolívar proposed a Federation of the Andes uniting Colombia, Peru and Bolivia. Peru would have been split into North and South states with Lima and Arequipa as capitals, and its southern coast, including Arica and Tarapacá, would have gone to Bolivia. Peru rejected the plan and it failed.
While withdrawing from Bolivarian influence, the Peruvian army under Agustín Gamarra entered Bolivia and forced Sucre to resign from the presidency. This ended Colombian influence in that country.

In 1908 around one hundred and twenty Peruvian soldiers were sent to Putumayo to help Arana's Peruvian Amazon Company expel the Colombians. The force raided and burned La Reserva and La Union, then threatened the inhabitants of El Dorado with death if they did not flee.

In 1832, Venezuelan president General José Antonio Páez passed an act making the University of the Andes a secular institution. Until then it had kept its affiliation with the Catholic Church, having begun as a Catholic seminary in 1785.

In 1883 the Venezuelan government reviewed the law on higher and scientific national education. The country's two existing universities were renamed, becoming Universidad de Los Andes in Mérida and Universidad Central de Venezuela in Caracas.

politics.text: On August 1, 1888, the university's Chancellor, Dr. Caracciolo Parra, issued a decree as part of a wave of institutional revampment. The University Library was at last inaugurated on October 27, 1889.

politics.text: In 1890 and 1891, the Colombian government protested in both Quito and Lima. It argued that the treaty interfered with its claims in the Napo and Amazon rivers.

philosophy.text: In 1810 a Catholic seminary in Mérida, in the Venezuelan Andes, was raised to the Royal University of San Buenaventura of Mérida. It could now confer degrees in Philosophy, Medicine, Civil and Canonical Law, and Theology. The seminary had been founded in 1785 by Bishop Juan Ramos de Lora.

Alexander von Humboldt's 1845 treatise Kosmos held that art is among the highest expressions of the love of nature. In its second volume he described how landscape painting influences the study of the natural world. He challenged artists to portray the "physiognomy" of the landscape.

The Mapuche deity Ngünechen, sometimes equated with the Christian God, first appeared in Mapuche religion during the 19th century. It has been argued that this deity was introduced in response to the Chilean national hierarchies. Some Mapuche traditionalists stress that Ngünechen and the Christian God are different.

The Peruvian poet and patriot Mariano Melgar was sent by his parents to Lima to study law at the age of twenty, and became very well educated in history, geography, philosophy and mathematics. In 1814 the revolution of Mateo Pumacahua in Cusco prompted him to join the independence cause, and he fought bravely directing the revolutionary army's artillery at the Battle of Umachiri on 11 March 1815. The patriots were defeated and made prisoners, including the young Melgar, and the Spanish General Ramirez ordered his officers to place him before a firing squad. Melgar was shot and died the next morning, 12 March 1815, at the age of 24.

A university charter for the Mérida seminary was granted in 1806. Because of the warlike period in the region, it was only validated in 1810, shortly before the Venezuelan Declaration of Independence. The seminary then became the Real Universidad de San Buenaventura de Mérida.

philosophy.text: In 1883 Venezuela reviewed its law on higher and scientific education, and the University of the Andes received that name. Its library was inaugurated on October 27, 1889. By the end of 1894 it held 1,436 titles and 1,725 volumes.

culture.text: When Frederic Edwin Church's huge painting The Heart of the Andes was later exhibited in other eastern U.S. cities, the exhibition rooms featured special lighting and decorative elements reminiscent of the landscape. At its 1859 New York debut, the public was willing to wait in line and pay a 25-cent entrance fee.

From 1849 to 1874, 80,000 to 100,000 Chinese contract laborers, 95% of them Cantonese and almost all male, were sent to Peru, mostly to sugar plantations, as slavery was being ended. They made a four-month trip from Macau and were meant to supply continuous labor for the coastal guano mines and plantations. They were believed to be reduced to virtual slaves, and those who stayed left a lasting cultural community whose members are called tusán.

In 1853 and 1857, Frederic Edwin Church traveled in Ecuador and Colombia, financed by businessman Cyrus West Field. Church was inspired by the Prussian naturalist Alexander von Humboldt and his 1845 treatise Kosmos. He retraced Humboldt's travels in South America.

San Martín de los Andes was founded on 4 February 1898 by Colonel Celestino Pérez as a military outpost to secure Argentine sovereignty amid border disputes with Chile. Its early economy was based on wood logging and husbandry. The town was modeled like a mountain village built with stone, wood and shingle roofs.

Church did not paint a single view in The Heart of the Andes. He synthesized numerous topographies of the Andes, from Mount Chimborazo to a plain and a jungle. Among the many details are animals and signs of human settlement, including people visiting a cross in the left foreground.

Chinese laborers in 19th-century Peru were barred from cemeteries reserved for Roman Catholics and were instead buried at pre-Incan burial sites. Between 1849 and 1874, half the Chinese population of Peru died from abuse, exhaustion and suicide caused by forced labor.

Before the town of San Martín de los Andes was founded, the indigenous Puelches used the Chapelco valley as a refuge in harsh winters. They raised horses on the eastern Andean slopes and traded them for weapons and alcoholic beverages. The Argentine and Chilean military campaigns of the second half of the 19th century, the conquest of the Desert and the occupation of Araucanía, ended this trade. In the 1880s the Argentine Army displaced indigenous communities.

Besides the plantation and guano mine workers, a third group of Chinese workers was contracted to build the railway from Lima to La Oroya and Huancayo. The coolies were believed to be reduced to virtual slaves, though they also represented a historical transition from slave to free labor. Between 1849 and 1874, half the Chinese population of Peru died from abuse, exhaustion and suicide caused by forced labor.

By the end of 1894, the University of the Andes library counted 1,436 titles and 1,725 volumes. By the turn of the 20th century these figures had grown to 2,120 titles and 2,572 volumes, despite a 19th century marked by political turmoil and coups d'état.
